gpt-mcpgw-run1.json|sourdough.why: It gives sound causes and fixes for dense sourdough and includes a source link.
gpt-mcpgw-run1.json|sourdough.answer:
Dense sourdough is usually **underproofed**: it didn’t ferment long enough to develop enough gas. Common causes include:

- **Weak or immature starter:** Use it when it’s risen, bubbly, loose, and sour-smelling.
- **Dough too cold:** Ferment it somewhere warmer or extend bulk fermentation.
- **Shaping too early:** Wait until the dough is puffy, jiggly, and visibly expanded; a quick-springing poke indicates it needs more time.
- **Too little water:** A stiff dough can produce a tight crumb—slightly increase hydration.
- **Gummy rather than dense:** Bake longer and cool at least 1–2 hours before slicing.

Also avoid relying strictly on recipe times; temperature and starter strength change fermentation speed.

Source: [Elevation Baking, “Why Is My Sourdough Dense?”](https://www.elevationbaking.com/adjustments/sourdough-dense-crumb)

claude-mcpgw-run1.json|sourdough.answer:
Most dense sourdough comes from fermentation or handling problems, not the recipe. The usual causes and fixes:

1. **Starter wasn't ready.** Feed it and wait until it visibly doubles and peaks before using it. A starter that takes 10–12 hours to double is too weak for a full loaf.
2. **Underfermented bulk.** Look for about 50–75% volume increase, bubbles, and a jiggly dough before shaping. Cold kitchens (below about 68°F) need a longer bulk.
3. **Overproofed.** If the loaf rose and then collapsed or spread, it fermented too long. Check it sooner next time.
4. **Gummy middle from an underbake or early slicing.** Bake until the interior reaches about 205–210°F on an instant-read thermometer, and let it cool before cutting.
5. **Weak shaping or a too-cool oven.** Tighten the dough when shaping, and preheat the Dutch oven 45–60 minutes so the loaf springs.

Fix one variable at a time and keep notes on starter activity, bulk temperature, and bake time.

Sources:
- Sourdough Savvy, "Why Is My Sourdough Dense? (8 Real Causes + Fixes)": https://sourdoughsavvy.com/why-is-my-sourdough-dense/ (main source for the list above)
- How to Make Sourdough, "Why Is My Sourdough Bread Dense? 7 Real Causes and How to Fix Each One": https://howtomakesourdough.com/overproofed-sourdough/why-is-my-sourdough-bread-dense/ (I only saw its search snippet; the fetched text was mismatched, so I didn't rely on it)

I couldn't open the Stack Overflow page itself (it returned HTTP 403), so this comes from search results and secondary sources.

**Author:** Mysticial appears to have written the top answer. A secondary summary of the thread credits "answers by Mysticial" first among the contributors ([caspimind.com](https://caspimind.com/videos/why-sorted-arrays-are-faster/)). I haven't confirmed the vote counts, so treat "top" as likely rather than verified.

**Main explanation:** Branch prediction. The loop's `if (data[c] >= 128)` branch is unpredictable on random data, so the CPU mispredicts often (roughly half the time), and each misprediction flushes the instruction pipeline. Sorted data makes the condition true for one long run and then false for another, so the predictor is almost always right. The question's own text is consistent with this: it's about conditional processing of a sorted versus unsorted array ([stackoverflow.com](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11227809/why-is-conditional-processing-of-a-sorted-array-faster-than-of-an-unsorted-array)).

Sources:

claude-mcpgw-run2.json|sourdough.answer:
Dense sourdough usually comes from a fermentation or handling problem, not the recipe. The most common causes are:

- **Underproofing:** the dough didn't rise enough before baking. This can come from a weak or unready starter, or cold dough.
- **Overproofing:** the dough fermented too long, lost its ability to hold gas, and collapsed or baked flat.
- **Weak shaping:** the loaf spread or lost surface tension during shaping.
- **Incomplete bake:** the loaf was underbaked, or sliced while still hot and gummy.
- **Flour or hydration:** whole grain flour or changed flour/water weights can give a heavier crumb.

**Fixes:**
- Use a starter that has visibly doubled after feeding before you mix.
- Mark the dough's starting level and check growth, rather than relying only on the clock.
- Shape more firmly to build surface tension.
- Bake fully, preheating the oven and Dutch oven well, and let the loaf cool before judging the crumb.

Sources: [How To Make Sourdough, "Why Is My Sourdough Bread Dense?"](https://howtomakesourdough.com/overproofed-sourdough/why-is-my-sourdough-bread-dense/) and the other search results it appeared with, such as [Flourwise](https://flourwise.com/blog/why-is-my-sourdough-dense/).

Note: when I fetched the How To Make Sourdough link, the returned text was from a different site (flexsourdough.com), so the causes above are checked against that text. I didn't verify the rest of the pages in full.

I couldn't confirm who wrote the top answer. Stack Overflow returned HTTP 403 when I tried to open the question, and the mirror sites I found don't name the answer's author.

The main explanation is **branch prediction**. The question's code sums values above a threshold. On a sorted array, the `if (x > threshold)` branch is true for a long unbroken run, so the CPU predicts it almost perfectly. On a random array, the outcome flips unpredictably, so the predictor is wrong about half the time, and each misprediction flushes the pipeline. Secondary sources agree on this. The question also notes that caching was ruled out, since the array was just generated.
